11.explanation: Comments document code rationale and logic without affecting machine execution.

11.question: What is a stub in software testing?
options: A syntax error in a function header
A physical break in an ethernet cable
A simple dummy subroutine that stands in for an unwritten module during top-down development
A full release version of a program
11.explanation: Stubs return predefined dummy values so higher-level modules can be tested before lower ones are coded.

11.question: What is an IDE (Integrated Development Environment)?
options: A hardware interface connecting storage drives to motherboards
A software suite providing comprehensive tools (source code editor, debugger, compiler/interpreter) for software development
An internet browser used for web design
11.explanation: IDEs combine code editors, build automation tools, syntax highlighting, and debuggers into a unified GUI.

12.question: What is the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)?
options: A structured framework defining the stages involved in the development, testing, deployment, and maintenance of software
The process of manufacturing computer processors
The time it takes for a hard drive to wear out
The warranty period provided by a software vendor
12.explanation: The SDLC guides software projects systematically from initial requirements analysis to retirement.

12.question: What is the first formal stage of the traditional Software Development Life Cycle?
12.explanation: Analysis investigates user needs, problem constraints, and feasibility before design begins.

12.question: What occurs during the Design stage of the SDLC?
options: Writing source code in a programming language
Deploying the software to end users
Planning software architecture, user interfaces, data structures, algorithms, and database schemas
Fixing bugs found in live production
12.explanation: Design translates requirements specifications into technical models, wireframes, and pseudocode algorithms.

12.question: What occurs during the Implementation (Coding) stage of the SDLC?
options: Translating software designs and algorithms into executable programs using a programming language
12.explanation: Implementation writes, documents, and compiles the source code based on design specifications.

12.question: What occurs during the Testing stage of the SDLC?
options: Executing the program with systematic test cases to find defects and verify it meets requirements
12.explanation: Testing validates system behavior against functional and non-functional requirements.

12.question: What occurs during the Maintenance stage of the SDLC?
options: Updating, modifying, and fixing software after it has been deployed to users
Selecting programming languages for the project
Writing the initial software requirement specification
12.explanation: Maintenance addresses bug fixes, performance tuning, and evolving user requirements post-release.

12.question: What is corrective maintenance?
options: Fixing bugs and errors discovered in the software after it has been deployed into production
Refactoring code to improve future maintainability
Adding new requested features for clients
Adapting software for a newly upgraded operating system
12.explanation: Corrective maintenance repairs defects and errors reported during live operations.

12.question: What is adaptive maintenance?
options: Adding new features requested by marketing
Modifying software to keep it operational when its environment (e.g. OS, hardware, regulations) changes
Fixing existing logic errors in algorithms
12.explanation: Adaptive maintenance ensures compatibility with new platforms, operating systems, or legal regulations.

12.question: What is perfective maintenance?
options: Fixing crash bugs reported by users
Enhancing software performance, usability, or adding new desired features to improve user satisfaction
Migrating software to a different server
12.explanation: Perfective maintenance adds enhancements, improves speed, and refines user interfaces.

12.question: What is the Waterfall model of software development?
options: An iterative approach delivering working software in short sprints
A model where coding begins before analysis
A linear, sequential development methodology where each phase must be completed before the next begins
A method where users write their own code
12.explanation: The Waterfall model flows strictly downwards through distinct phases without revisiting prior steps easily.

12.question: What is an advantage of the Waterfall model?
options: Working software is delivered within the first few weeks
Clear structure, well-defined milestones, and thorough documentation at every stage
High flexibility to easily accommodate changing requirements late in development
12.explanation: Waterfall's rigid structure and documentation make it easy to manage when requirements are fixed and stable.

12.question: What is a major limitation of the Waterfall model?
options: It does not allow any documentation to be written
It can only be used for web development
It produces too many software releases
It is difficult and costly to accommodate changing user requirements once development is underway
12.explanation: Inflexibility makes Waterfall risky if user needs evolve or were misunderstood during early analysis.

12.question: What is the Iterative (Agile) model of software development?
options: A linear model where testing only happens at the very end
A model where hardware is manufactured alongside code
A flexible methodology where software is developed in rapid, repeating cycles (iterations/sprints) with frequent customer feedback
A model that eliminates all testing and documentation
12.explanation: Agile emphasizes adaptability, incremental progress, continuous testing, and active client collaboration.

12.question: What is an advantage of Agile development methodologies?
options: Detailed complete documentation is guaranteed upfront
High adaptability to evolving user requirements and regular delivery of functional software increments
Fixed budget and rigid unchanging deadlines
12.explanation: Agile delivers working versions quickly, allowing early user feedback to steer upcoming iterations.

12.question: What is the Spiral model of software development?
options: A model that only designs user interfaces
A risk-driven development model that combines iterative development with systematic risk assessment at each loop
A linear model with no feedback loops
A method of writing assembly language without compilers
12.explanation: The Spiral model repeatedly assesses project risks at every quadrant before proceeding to the next iteration.

12.question: What is Rapid Application Development (RAD)?
options: A development methodology emphasizing rapid prototyping, user feedback, and CASE tools rather than extensive upfront planning
A method focused purely on writing formal mathematical proofs
A model that requires years of analysis before prototyping
A process that avoids using graphical interfaces
12.explanation: RAD uses interactive workshops, prototyping tools, and reusable components for fast turnaround.

12.question: What is a prototype in software development?
options: A legal contract between developers and clients
The final packaged release shipped to stores
A software defect that causes system crashes
An early, working model or preview of a software system used to demonstrate concepts and gather user feedback
12.explanation: Prototypes give stakeholders tangible previews to validate requirements before full-scale coding.

12.question: What is an evolutionary prototype?
options: A prototype that is completely discarded after requirements are gathered
A prototype used to test hardware circuits only
A prototype written exclusively in machine code
A prototype that is incrementally refined, expanded, and tested until it becomes the final production system
12.explanation: Evolutionary prototypes form the actual foundation of the eventual product through iterative expansion.

12.question: What is a throwaway (throw-away) prototype?
options: A quick, rudimentary model built solely to clarify requirements or test feasibility, discarded after evaluation
A backup copy of source code
A software version that is sold at a discount
12.explanation: Throwaway prototypes explore risky technical ideas or ambiguous requirements and are then rewritten cleanly.

12.question: What is white-box (structural) testing?
options: Testing conducted exclusively by external end users
Testing that evaluates internal program logic, code structure, and execution paths with full access to source code
Testing the physical cleanliness of server rooms
Testing software without knowledge of the internal code or implementation
12.explanation: White-box testing inspects internal control structures, branches, conditions, and paths.

12.question: What is black-box (functional) testing?
options: Testing internal algorithm code line by line
Testing conducted exclusively in dark computer labs
Testing that treats the software as an opaque box, testing inputs and outputs without examining internal code
12.explanation: Black-box testing focuses purely on whether software inputs yield expected outputs against specifications.

12.question: What is unit testing?
options: Testing the software on multiple physical computers across a LAN
Testing individual software modules, functions, or subroutines in isolation to verify correct behavior
Testing user acceptance during live deployment
Testing the complete integrated software system as a whole
12.explanation: Unit tests verify discrete units of source code independently using test harnesses and stubs.

12.question: What is integration testing?
options: Testing an individual function in complete isolation
Testing that verifies that different software modules or subsystems interact and exchange data correctly
Testing software by asking end users to grade it
12.explanation: Integration testing reveals interface bugs when combining independently developed modules.

12.question: What is system testing?
options: Testing a single loop in a subroutine
Testing hardware memory chips with a diagnostic tool
Testing network cabling for signal loss
Testing the complete, fully integrated software application to verify that it meets all specified requirements
12.explanation: System testing validates end-to-end functionality, performance, and security across the entire application.

12.question: What is Alpha testing?
options: Testing conducted by in-house developers and internal QA staff in a controlled development environment
Testing hardware components on a test bench
Testing conducted by a large group of external end users in their real environments
Testing software after it has been commercially released
12.explanation: Alpha testing is the initial internal testing phase performed by the development organization.

12.question: What is Beta testing?
options: Testing executed after retiring an application
Internal testing performed strictly by the original programmers
Automated syntax checking performed by a compiler
Testing conducted by a targeted group of real external end users in their own operating environments before release
12.explanation: Beta testing exposes the near-final product to real-world usage conditions to catch edge-case bugs.

12.question: What is Acceptance testing?
options: Testing code for compiler syntax errors
Formal testing conducted to determine whether the software satisfies client criteria and is accepted for delivery
12.explanation: Acceptance testing proves to the customer/stakeholder that contractual requirements are fulfilled.

12.question: What is regression testing?
options: Re-running previous tests after code modifications to ensure that existing functionality has not been broken
Testing only the user interface design
Testing software on older legacy hardware
Deleting old test cases to save disk space
12.explanation: Regression testing ensures that bug fixes or new features have not inadvertently created new defects.

12.question: What is a test plan?
options: A list of employee payroll numbers
A contract with a hardware supplier
A comprehensive document outlining the scope, approach, resources, schedule, and test cases for software testing
12.explanation: Test plans detail what features will be tested, testing strategies, test environments, and pass/fail criteria.

12.question: What key components make up a well-designed test case?
options: Operating system license key and serial number
Source code comments, compiler version, and author photo
Test ID, test description, test data/inputs, expected result, actual result, and pass/fail status
12.explanation: Test cases specify exact inputs and expected outputs so results can be evaluated objectively.

12.question: What is a debugger?
options: A hardware cleaner that blows dust out of cooling fans
A tool that automatically writes source code
An antivirus program that deletes malware files
A software development tool that allows programmers to inspect program execution, set breakpoints, and trace variables
12.explanation: Debuggers help developers pinpoint logic and runtime errors by stepping through executing code.

12.question: What is a breakpoint in a debugger?
options: A comment line in source code
A point where the program crashes permanently
The end of a loop construct
A deliberate stopping point set in code where program execution pauses so internal states can be inspected
12.explanation: Breakpoints pause execution at specific lines, allowing developers to inspect variable values in memory.

12.question: What does 'single-stepping' (step-into / step-over) mean in a debugger?
options: Skipping all subroutines without running them
Compiling only one file at a time
Running the program at double clock speed
Executing source code line-by-line under developer control to observe state changes after each instruction
12.explanation: Stepping executes one instruction at a time, revealing precisely when a variable acquires an unexpected value.

12.question: What is a variable watch (watch window) in a debugger?
options: A debugging feature that tracks and displays the current value of specified variables as code executes
A digital clock displayed on the taskbar
A timer that shuts down idle computers
12.explanation: Watches monitor critical variables in real time, alerting developers when values change unexpectedly.

12.question: What is version control (e.g. Git)?
options: A system that records changes to files over time, enabling team collaboration, tracking history, and reverting code
12.explanation: Version control tracks source code revisions, supports branching/merging, and maintains project history.

12.question: What is a code repository?
options: A physical warehouse storing computer motherboards
A trash bin for deleted software files
A server used solely for streaming video
A central storage location where source code, documentation, and revision history are managed
12.explanation: Repositories (local or remote) organize all project assets and commit logs for collaborative access.

12.question: What is direct changeover (cutover) implementation?
options: Completely stopping the old system and switching immediately to the new system on a chosen date
Testing the system in one branch before expanding
Running both old and new systems simultaneously for a transition period
Introducing the new system one department or module at a time
12.explanation: Direct changeover is immediate; it has low initial cost but carries high risk if the new system fails.

12.question: What is an advantage of direct changeover?
options: It is quick, avoids duplicating data entry across systems, and requires fewer resources than parallel running
It carries zero risk of system failure
The old system remains available as an automatic live backup
Users do not require any training
12.explanation: Direct changeover eliminates maintaining two systems simultaneously, saving time and operating overhead.

12.question: What is a major disadvantage of direct changeover?
options: It requires double the computer hardware
High risk; if the new system fails or experiences critical bugs, there is no operational backup system available
It takes months to complete the transition
Staff must enter data twice every day
12.explanation: Without a fallback, catastrophic failures in the new system can halt business operations entirely.

12.question: What is parallel running implementation?
options: Shutting down the old system overnight and booting the new one
Releasing one module of software each month
Running the old and new systems side-by-side for a period until the new system proves reliable
Implementing the system in one branch office only
12.explanation: Parallel running provides maximum safety by comparing outputs from both systems concurrently.

12.question: What is an advantage of parallel running?
options: It requires no extra staff workload
It finishes faster than any other method
It is the cheapest changeover method
Very low risk; if the new system fails, the old system continues uninterrupted without data loss
12.explanation: Parallel operation guarantees business continuity and allows direct validation of new system outputs.

12.question: What is a disadvantage of parallel running?
options: High cost and double workload for staff who must enter all transactions into both systems
If the new system fails, the entire company ceases operation
It cannot be tested prior to changeover
12.explanation: Staff must duplicate data entry and operations, increasing operational expenses and potential fatigue.

12.question: What is phased (staged) implementation?
options: Switching all company branches to the new system at once
Introducing the new system in progressive stages or modules over time while phasing out old modules
Testing the software on a single computer only
12.explanation: Phased implementation deploys individual components (e.g. billing, then inventory) step-by-step.
